items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “an issue that affects people in many parts of the world and cannot be solved by one country acting alone”?
options: Sovereignty
Intergovernmental organisation
Global issue
Global dimension
items.answer: Global issue
items.markingKey: Global issue: an issue that affects people in many parts of the world and cannot be solved by one country acting alone. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): The spread of election disinformation is a global issue. Reason (R): Social media platforms operate across national borders. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Both true; cross-border platforms are why the issue is global. [1]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Climate migration is only a national issue. Reason (R): Most people displaced by climate change move within their own country. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: A is false: it also has global dimensions (cross-border migration, no international legal status). R is broadly true: most displacement is internal. [1]

items.stem: Read this extract from a community newsletter in Lisbon: “Residents are concerned about a community group in a war-affected town waiting for UN peacekeepers who are not sent.” Explain one way in which a course of action by the UN member states could affect the local community.
items.answer: If the UN member states decided to abolish or restrict the veto for cases of mass atrocities, the community would feel the effect: it would stop one country blocking action to prevent genocide; however the permanent members would have to agree, and they can veto Charter amendments.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies effect; 1 mark explains link from national/global action to local [2]

items.stem: A student in Singapore reads a report about false rumours about polling station closures shared in a community messaging group. (a) Identify the local dimension of the issue described. (b) Explain one way in which a course of action by the national government could affect the local community.
items.answer: (a) False rumours about polling station closures shared in a community messaging group. (b) If the national government decided to require platforms to label and remove false political content, the community would feel the effect: it reduces the reach of the most harmful falsehoods quickly; however governments or companies may use it to silence legitimate criticism.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for the local example [1] (b) 1 mark identifies effect; 1 mark explains link from national/global action to local [2]

items.stem: A student in Nairobi reads a report about farmers downstream noticing lower river levels during the dry season. (a) Suggest one national dimension of disputes over shared rivers. (b) Suggest why action at a local level alone may not solve the issue.
items.answer: (a) A government building a large hydroelectric dam to supply electricity to millions of homes. (b) The causes are partly national and global (population growth increases demand for water and food), so local action cannot change them; national laws and international cooperation are also needed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark national example; 1 mark explains link to government or laws [2] (b) 1 mark cause outside local control; 1 mark need for wider action [2]

items.stem: What is meant by “global issue” in Global Perspectives?
options: The authority of a state to govern itself without outside interference.
The growing interconnection of economies, cultures and societies through trade, travel, migration and communication.
The way an issue affects a whole country and is dealt with by its government and laws.
An issue that affects people in many parts of the world and cannot be solved by one country acting alone.
items.answer: An issue that affects people in many parts of the world and cannot be solved by one country acting alone.
items.markingKey: Global issue: an issue that affects people in many parts of the world and cannot be solved by one country acting alone. [1]

items.stem: A revision blog states: “Globalisation has made countries more interdependent.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. Trade, finance, migration and communication link countries, so events in one place affect others.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Sovereignty can make global issues harder to solve. Reason (R): States can refuse to accept international agreements. Choose the correct option.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: Both true and R explains A. [1]

items.stem: Explain why disputes over shared rivers can be described as a global issue.
items.answer: National: A government building a large hydroelectric dam to supply electricity to millions of homes. Global: More than 260 river basins shared by two or more countries, with weak international law on how to share the water. Because causes and effects cross borders, no single government can solve it alone.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies a cross-border cause or effect; 1 mark develops with an example; 1 mark explains why international cooperation is needed [3]

items.stem: A report from Lagos describes false rumours about polling station closures shared in a community messaging group. The issue is part of a wider debate about the spread of online disinformation during elections. Explain why this issue also has a global dimension.
items.answer: Foreign governments and networks using social media platforms that operate across borders to influence elections in other countries.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cross-border cause/effect; 1 mark developed with example [2]

items.stem: Noah, a student in Doha, is investigating threats to press freedom after noticing a local reporter threatened after exposing a council official’s links to a building firm. (a) Explain why this issue also has a global dimension. (b) Suggest why action at a local level alone may not solve the issue.
items.answer: (a) Journalists jailed or killed in many countries, recorded each year by Reporters Without Borders and the Committee to Protect Journalists. (b) The causes are partly national and global (governments want to control criticism before elections), so local action cannot change them; national laws and international cooperation are also needed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark cross-border cause/effect; 1 mark developed with example [2] (b) 1 mark cause outside local control; 1 mark need for wider action [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that the use of economic sanctions can only be solved through international cooperation. You may wish to consider: evidence of what has worked; sovereignty; local, national and global dimensions.
items.answer: For: Sanctions imposed by the UN Security Council, the EU or the USA affecting trade and finance around the world. Possible international action: use targeted (“smart”) sanctions on named individuals and firms (UN Security Council or regional bodies). Against: Much of the problem is national or local: an economy in recession after its oil exports are restricted. National or local action such as to allow humanitarian exemptions for food and medicine can make a difference: they reduce harm to civilians. Judgement: International cooperation is necessary for the cross-border dimensions, but most effective responses combine it with national and local action.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: Using the export of plastic waste to poorer countries as an example, explain how one global issue can involve more than one topic area.
items.answer: It is linked to Sustainable living, but it also has a social side (“consumers in rich countries use large amounts of single-use plastic”) and a technological side (“mixed plastics are hard to recycle”); governments must decide how to respond, so it is also a political and governance issue.

items.stem: A report from Doha describes families in a coastal village moving inland after repeated flooding. The issue is part of a wider debate about migration caused by climate change. Suggest one piece of evidence a student could look for to judge how serious the issue is.
items.answer: For example, data on how many people experience families in a coastal village moving inland after repeated flooding, or on pressure on housing and services in the cities that receive migrants.
items.markingKey: 1 mark relevant evidence; 1 mark explains what it would show [2]

items.stem: Explain whether you agree that threats to press freedom is better understood as a political issue than as an issue of technology or society. Give one reason for and one reason against.
items.answer: For: Governments and international bodies decide the rules and the response. For example, parliament could protect journalists’ sources and repeal broad “false news” laws. Against: Its causes include media owners have business links with ruling parties, which is not mainly political. Non-state actors such as businesses, NGOs and individuals also shape it. Judgement: The issue is best understood across topic areas; politics shapes the response but other factors drive the causes.

items.answer: It is linked to Migration and work, but it also has a environmental side (“repeated droughts destroy the livelihoods of farmers”) and a economic side (“poorer countries lack funds to build flood defences”); governments must decide how to respond, so it is also a political and governance issue.

items.stem: Tariq, a student in Manila, is investigating the under-representation of women in parliaments after noticing a municipal council in which only two of twenty councillors are women. (a) Identify one social factor that contributes to the issue. (b) Explain why governments are involved in responding to this issue.
items.answer: (a) Women carry more unpaid caring work, leaving less time for politics. (b) Governments make laws and policies, for example a parliament could introduce legal candidate quotas requiring parties to field a minimum share of women; Rwanda, which has reserved seats for women, has had a female majority in its lower house since 2008.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 1 mark identifies government action; 1 mark explains its purpose [2]

items.stem: A newspaper column asserts: “If a national government passes a law on an issue, the issue is no longer global.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. A national law addresses the national dimension; cross-border causes and effects remain and need cooperation.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate supporting explanation [2]

items.stem: Read this extract from a local newspaper in Karachi: “Residents are concerned about a pharmacy unable to import medicines because banks will not process payments.” Explain why this issue also has a global dimension.
items.answer: Sanctions imposed by the UN Security Council, the EU or the USA affecting trade and finance around the world.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cross-border cause/effect; 1 mark developed with example [2]

items.stem: Read this extract from a podcast episode in Lima: “Residents are concerned about a city road contract awarded to a company owned by a councillor’s relative.” Explain why this issue also has a global dimension.
items.answer: Bribes paid by multinational companies to win contracts abroad and money hidden in offshore financial centres.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cross-border cause/effect; 1 mark developed with example [2]

items.stem: A report from Accra describes a city road contract awarded to a company owned by a councillor’s relative. The issue is part of a wider debate about corruption in public procurement. (a) Identify the local dimension of the issue described. (b) Suggest one national dimension of corruption in public procurement.
items.answer: (a) A city road contract awarded to a company owned by a councillor’s relative. (b) Public money lost on overpriced hospital and school building contracts.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for the local example [1] (b) 1 mark national example; 1 mark explains link to government or laws [2]

items.stem: A report from Istanbul describes a city installing facial recognition cameras in a busy shopping street. The issue is part of a wider debate about state use of facial recognition surveillance. (a) Suggest one national dimension of state use of facial recognition surveillance. (b) Suggest why action at a local level alone may not solve the issue.
items.answer: (a) A national police database of facial images built without a specific law authorising it. (b) The causes are partly national and global (the cost of cameras and computing power has fallen sharply), so local action cannot change them; national laws and international cooperation are also needed.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark national example; 1 mark explains link to government or laws [2] (b) 1 mark cause outside local control; 1 mark need for wider action [2]

items.stem: Sipho, a student in Santiago, is investigating corruption in public procurement after noticing a city road contract awarded to a company owned by a councillor’s relative. (a) Suggest one national dimension of corruption in public procurement. (b) Suggest why action at a local level alone may not solve the issue. (c) Explain one way in which a course of action by the national government could affect the local community.
items.answer: (a) Public money lost on overpriced hospital and school building contracts. (b) The causes are partly national and global (officials have wide discretion and little oversight when awarding contracts), so local action cannot change them; national laws and international cooperation are also needed. (c) If the national government decided to publish all public contracts online (open contracting), the community would feel the effect: citizens, journalists and rival firms can spot suspicious deals; however publication alone does not punish anyone.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark national example; 1 mark explains link to government or laws [2] (b) 1 mark cause outside local control; 1 mark need for wider action [2] (c) 1 mark identifies effect; 1 mark explains link from national/global action to local [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person, set out in documents such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948)”?
options: Democracy
Human rights
Civil society
Governance
items.answer: Human rights
items.markingKey: Human rights: basic rights and freedoms that belong to every person, set out in documents such as the Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948). [1]

items.stem: Using the under-representation of women in parliaments as an example, explain how one global issue can involve more than one topic area.
items.answer: It is linked to Political and governance issues, but it also has a social side (“women politicians face more online abuse”) and a political side (“parties choose men for safe seats more often than women”), so it reaches beyond formal politics into other topic areas such as society and the economy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies one topic area; 1 mark a second area with an example from the issue; 1 mark explains the link [3]

items.stem: Using lowering the voting age to 16 as an example, explain how one global issue can involve more than one topic area.
items.answer: It is linked to Political and governance issues, but it also has a political side (“youth campaign groups have become better organised”) and a economic side (“16-year-olds can already work and pay tax in many countries”), so it reaches beyond formal politics into other topic areas such as society and the economy.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies one topic area; 1 mark a second area with an example from the issue; 1 mark explains the link [3]

items.stem: A report from Bogotá describes a city installing facial recognition cameras in a busy shopping street. The issue is part of a wider debate about state use of facial recognition surveillance. Explain why governments are involved in responding to this issue.
items.answer: Governments make laws and policies, for example a parliament could ban live facial recognition in public places; it protects privacy and freedom of assembly.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies government action; 1 mark explains its purpose [2]

items.stem: Zara argues that low voter turnout among young people is better understood as a political issue than as an issue of technology or society. How far do you agree? Support your answer with reasoning and evidence.
items.answer: For: Governments and international bodies decide the rules and the response. For example, national government could make voting compulsory, with a small fine for non-voters. Against: Its causes include young people feel that political parties ignore issues that matter to them, which is not mainly political. Non-state actors such as businesses, NGOs and individuals also shape it. Judgement: The issue is best understood across topic areas; politics shapes the response but other factors drive the causes.
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1–2 marks): simple, one-sided assertions with little support. Level 2 (3–4 marks): explains arguments on one side well, or both sides in less depth, using some evidence or examples. Level 3 (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of different perspectives, evidence evaluated for quality, and a reasoned, supported judgement on “to what extent”. [6]

items.stem: What is meant by “closed question” in Global Perspectives?
options: A question to which reasonable people can give different answers supported by evidence.
The range of places, groups and time covered by an enquiry.
A question with a single factual or yes/no answer that leaves no room for debate.
A focused question that guides research into an issue.
items.answer: A question with a single factual or yes/no answer that leaves no room for debate.
items.markingKey: Closed question: a question with a single factual or yes/no answer that leaves no room for debate. [1]

items.stem: A student proposes this enquiry question: “How many countries are affected by the spread of online disinformation during elections?” What is its main weakness?
options: It is too broad to research in depth
It has no global dimension and no room for different perspectives
It is a leading question that assumes the answer
It is a closed, factual question with no room for debate
items.answer: It is a closed, factual question with no room for debate
items.markingKey: It is a closed, factual question with no room for debate. [1]

items.stem: Explain why “How can global politics be improved?” is not an effective question for a Global Perspectives enquiry.
items.answer: It is too broad to research in depth: it covers far too many issues and places to research in depth within an essay.
items.markingKey: 1 mark identifies the weakness; 1 mark explains why it limits the enquiry [2]

items.stem: Felix writes this question for an enquiry: “Why is it obvious that economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour?” Rewrite it as an effective, debatable question about the use of economic sanctions and explain why your version is better.
items.answer: For example: “Are economic sanctions an effective way to change a government’s behaviour?” This is focused on one issue, open to different answers and perspectives, and has a clear global dimension; the original is a leading question that assumes the answer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark focused, open question; 1 mark debatable/allows perspectives; 1 mark explains the improvement [3]

items.stem: Elena writes this question for an enquiry: “How can global politics be improved?” Rewrite it as an effective, debatable question about the spread of online disinformation during elections and explain why your version is better.
items.answer: For example: “Should social media companies be legally responsible for false political content on their platforms?” This is focused on one issue, open to different answers and perspectives, and has a clear global dimension; the original is too broad to research in depth.
items.markingKey: 1 mark focused, open question; 1 mark debatable/allows perspectives; 1 mark explains the improvement [3]

items.stem: Ana writes this question for an enquiry: “Why do only selfish people oppose the view that economic sanctions are rarely an effective way to change a government’s behaviour?” Rewrite it as an effective, debatable question about the use of economic sanctions and explain why your version is better.
items.answer: For example: “Are economic sanctions an effective way to change a government’s behaviour?” This is focused on one issue, open to different answers and perspectives, and has a clear global dimension; the original is a leading question that assumes the answer.
items.markingKey: 1 mark focused, open question; 1 mark debatable/allows perspectives; 1 mark explains the improvement [3]

items.stem: Three students suggest questions about the under-representation of women in parliaments: Question X: “Are gender quotas the best way to increase the number of women in parliament?” Question Y: “Why do only selfish people oppose the view that countries should introduce legal gender quotas for parliament?” Question Z: “What is wrong with the world’s approach to political and governance issues?” (a) Identify the question that is most suitable for a Global Perspectives essay. (b) Explain the weakness of the other two questions.
items.answer: (a) Question X. (b) One is weak because it is too broad to research in depth; the other because it is a leading question that assumes the answer.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark [1] (b) 2 marks for each weakness explained [4]
